query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding approximately 1 atomic percent silicon to the equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, silica-rich protective surface scale during high-temperature air exposure, thereby improving its oxidation resistance (preventing pesting) while maintaining its established mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy in its as-cast state with known inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Minor compositional tuning via the addition of ~1 at% Si into the base alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at high temperatures (between 800 °C and 1000 °C) for about 5 hours; subsequent mechanical tests consistent with room-temperature tensile ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength evaluation (e.g., at 1000 °C, strain rates 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1)).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, continuous SiO2 (silica-rich) scale at the alloy surface during high-temperature oxidation.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, trace silicon reacts with oxygen to form a dense silica layer that acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion, thus reducing pesting and oxidation without altering the bulk microstructure responsible for the alloy’s mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated equiatomic alloy, the Si-doped variant will exhibit enhanced oxidation resistance (i.e., limited pesting and reduced oxidation penetration) while retaining its useful room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: The untreated equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy, which displays 8–16% tensile ductility at room temperature and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance during high-temperature exposure in air.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to annealing/exposure conditions at 800–1000 °C in ambient air for ~5 hours; mechanical performance is considered under the strain rates of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1) with testing at room temperature and elevated temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: Although similar trace reactive-element additions in related non-equiatomic alloys have improved oxidation resistance, it remains uncertain whether 1 at% Si will not inadvertently alter the microstructure or degrade the mechanical properties of the equiatomic composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr and a second set modified with 1 at% Si. Expose both sets to identical conditions in air (e.g., 800 °C and 1000 °C for 5 hours). After exposure, examine the surface oxide layers using SEM/TEM and quantify the oxidation penetration depth. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature yield strength tests (using strain rates between 10^(-4) and 10^(-2) s^(-1)).
measurements: Oxide scale continuity and composition (via SEM, EDS, and TEM)
Microstructural analysis to detect unwanted phase changes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the Si-added alloy does not develop a continuous, protective silica-rich scale or if its oxidation resistance is not significantly improved compared to the untreated alloy, or if the addition of Si results in a statistically significant degradation of room-temperature ductility or high-temperature yield strength.

cited_evidence.text: Structural metallic materials for applications at high temperatures must have a balance of mechanical properties and oxidation resistance. Coated and internally cooled Ni-based superalloys are used in gas turbine engines close to their high temperature limit, which is imposed by the melting temperature of Ni. The search for new alloys with similar or better capabilities at higher temperatures has concentrated on Nb-silicide based alloys that have lower densities, significantly higher solidus temperatures in excess of 1900 °C and can offer notable mechanical properties []. For example, some of these alloys can have compressive yield strength of about 1800 MPa at room temperature, 1200 MPa at 1000 °C and 500 MPa at 1200 °C []. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. decision.trend: The earlier work on refractory high‐entropy alloys, especially studies on equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, focused on establishing their baseline mechanical performance and understanding microstructural influences after casting. In parallel, oxidation‐protection research on non‐equiatomic variants demonstrated that minor compositional modifications can suppress pesting and oxidation (for example, by introducing a trace reactive element that forms a protective oxide scale). However, while researchers have tuned compositions for strength and ductility, they have not yet directly addressed the oxidation resistance issue in the equiatomic alloy.
decision.unsolved: Even though the related non‐equiatomic alloy showed prevention of pesting at 800 °C for 5 hours, the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr remains vulnerable to oxygen attack at high temperatures. The challenge is to achieve a single intervention that protects against oxidation (pesting) under aggressive air exposure while fully preserving the alloy’s useful room- and high-temperature mechanical properties.
decision.lever: minor compositional tuning via trace reactive-element addition (≈1 at% Si)
decision.why: Based on the trend of first establishing the baseline mechanical performance of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and then exploring compositional modifications in related systems to curb oxidation, the most plausible next step is the controlled introduction of a trace reactive element. Adding about 1 atomic percent silicon is expected to form a thin, continuous silica layer during high-temperature air exposure (800–1000 °C for ~5 h), which protects against oxygen ingress while minimally affecting the microstructure and mechanical integrity. This approach aligns with the niche move emphasizing a targeted, minimal composition modification to extend oxidation resistance, and it is supported by prior studies on related alloys that used similar strategies.
